whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Sooner Rather Than Later

items.title: California's Filing Deadline
items.desc: You generally have two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury claim in California, though claims against a government agency can require notice in as little as six months. Waiting too long can mean losing your right to recover anything.

items.title: Partial Fault Doesn't Bar Recovery
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning even if you were partly responsible for the crash, you can still recover compensation reduced by your share of fault. An attorney can help make sure fault is assessed fairly.

items.title: No Cap on Non-Economic Damages
items.desc: In ordinary injury cases, California places no cap on damages for pain, suffering, and other non-economic losses. That makes a thorough case evaluation especially worthwhile.

items.title: No Fee Unless You Recover
items.desc: Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so you don't pay out of pocket to get advice or representation. Fees only come from a settlement or award if your case succeeds.

items.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in California?
items.answer: In most cases you have two years from the date of the injury to file a lawsuit. If your claim involves a government entity, such as a city vehicle, the notice period can be as short as six months, so it's best not to wait.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to happen in Willows?
items.answer: Public collision records show higher activity along corridors like Interstate 5 Northbound, W Wood Street, Sycamore Street, and Rt 162, with reports peaking on Wednesdays between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. These are simply reported counts, not a judgment about any road's safety.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.answer: California uses pure comparative fault, which means you can still recover compensation even if you share some responsibility. Your recovery would be reduced by your percentage of fault, but it isn't eliminated.

items.question: Is there a limit on how much I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: No, California does not cap non-economic damages like pain and suffering in standard personal injury cases. Every case is different, and an attorney can explain what factors matter for your situation.

items.question: Does it cost anything to talk to an attorney through LawProactive?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service, and we are not a law firm ourselves — we simply help connect you with an independent attorney. Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so they only get paid if you recover compensation.
